correctness.rationale: Vijayan et al. Eqs. (30), (33)–(34), and (44) give the squared lag, averaged excess dissipation, and normalized ratio; substituting with (nπ)^8=λ_n⁴ yields the frozen Q_n exactly. For B=cosh s−cos s>0, the numerator is sA(s), with A(0)=0 and A′(s)=s(sinh s−sin s)>0. An independent expansion gives F(s)=s⁴/30−s⁸/14175+O(s¹⁰) and exponential factoring gives F(s)=(s²−s)/2+O(s²e^(−s)). Hence E=s²/(2F)≤const(1+s⁻²), Q_n tends to 1 at zero frequency and 0 at infinity, and Q_n(rλ_n)/λ_n=(8/135)h(r)E(nπ√(r/2)). The lower and upper r tails are uniformly O(η+1/λ_n) and O(1/R), respectively, so all large-n maxima exist and lie in a compact interval. The independently checked numerator of h′ is −r⁶−88r⁴−528r²+2304, strictly decreasing in r²; its only positive root gives the strictly curved unique limit. The large-s expansion with two derivatives yields h(r)[1+√2/(πn√r)+O(n⁻²)] near this limit, up to the overall prefactor. The stationary equation yields the stated negative δ_*; local strict concavity, with exclusion of the rest of the compact interval, gives eventual uniqueness. Substitution gives C_* and D_*; independent high-precision values agree. The frozen script and recorded JSON were inspected, not executed; their finite bounded searches cannot justify global attainment or uniqueness. No claim extends beyond the specified continuum linear response.

value.rationale: A sharp global envelope establishes the size of the higher-mode failure in a model where selected modes were already known to exceed the slowest-mode bound. The asymptotic optimizing frequency and first corrections describe how to realize that sharp growth, rather than merely giving a lower bound by choosing one frequency. This is valuable within the continuum model, not evidence of finite-lattice or unnormalized-lag divergence.
